questions.question: A gust of wind sets a still beach ball rolling, and a fence stops it again. Scientists say a force acts on the ball each time. What is a force?
choices: A push or a pull
A burst of energy
A kind of motion
A kind of matter
questions.context: A force is a push or a pull that one thing gives another: the wind pushes the ball into motion, and the fence pushes back to stop it. A force is not energy, motion or matter, though it can change how a thing moves.
questions.grade_note: 'A force is a push or a pull' opens every 5th-grade forces unit (Florida SC.5.P.13.1 names pushes and pulls; TEKS 5.7A builds on it).

questions.question: Two teams heave on the ends of a rope in a tug-of-war. Both pull hard, yet the middle of the rope stays right where it is. What must happen for the rope to start moving?
questions.answer: One team must pull harder than the other
choices: One team must pull harder than the other
Both teams must pull harder than before
Both teams must keep pulling for longer
Gravity must stop holding the rope down
questions.context: While the two pulls are equal they are balanced, and balanced forces leave the rope's motion unchanged, however hard or long both teams pull. Once one team out-pulls the other the forces are unbalanced, and the rope moves toward the stronger side.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.7A has 5th graders explain how equal and unequal forces cause patterns of motion, and a tug-of-war is the standard picture of balanced forces.

questions.question: A boy at the top of a tall ladder lets go of a rock. Earth's gravity pulls on it the whole time it falls. How does the rock's speed change as it falls?
questions.answer: It speeds up all the way down
choices: It speeds up all the way down
It falls at one steady speed
It speeds up, then holds steady
It starts fast, then slows down
questions.context: Gravity is an unbalanced force on the falling rock, and an unbalanced force keeps changing an object's speed: near the ground a falling thing gains almost 10 metres per second of speed every second. Only a very long fall, far longer than this one, ever stops speeding up.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.13.1 names gravity acting on falling objects, and TEKS 5.7A teaches that an unequal force changes motion; a dropped thing speeding up is the plainest case.

questions.question: A boy kicks a soccer ball across a flat, grassy field. No player touches it again, yet it rolls slower and slower until it stops. What slows it down and stops it?
choices: Friction pushing against its motion
The force of his kick running out
Gravity pulling it back to a stop
Moving things stopping on their own
questions.context: The grass rubs against the rolling ball, and the air pushes on it too, both against its motion; that rubbing force, friction, slows it to a stop. A kick is a push that ends when the foot leaves the ball, so the ball holds no store of force to run out.
questions.grade_note: Friction as the force that slows moving things is part of upper-elementary forces work (TeachEngineering's grades 3-5 ramp activity; Oak National Academy's Year 5 friction lesson).

questions.question: Some students roll the same toy car down the same ramp twice: once onto smooth wood, once onto shaggy carpet. How will the car's two rolls across the floor compare?
questions.answer: Shorter on the carpet, which makes more friction
choices: Shorter on the carpet, which makes more friction
Shorter on the wood, which makes more friction
The same on both, since the ramp is the same
Longer on the carpet, which is soft and springy
questions.context: Friction is greater on rough surfaces, and the carpet's thick, uneven fibres drag on the wheels far more than smooth wood does, so the car stops much sooner there. The ramp starts the car off the same each time; the floor makes the difference.
questions.grade_note: A car on a ramp is the TEKS 5.7B investigation, and a car slowed most by a carpet's rough surface is its classic result (TeachEngineering, grades 3-5).

questions.question: A hockey puck slides straight north across a frozen pond. A player wants to make it swerve west with one tap of his stick. On which side of the puck should he push?
choices: Its east side
Its west side
Its south side
Its north side
questions.context: A push moves a thing the way the push points. A tap on the puck's east side pushes it west, so it swerves west; a tap on its west side would send it east, a tap from behind (the south) would only speed it up, and one from in front (the north) would slow it down.
questions.grade_note: That a force has a direction as well as a strength (NGSS PS2.A) is built on at grade 5, where TEKS 5.7A asks how unequal forces change an object's motion, turning included.

questions.question: Earth is round, and people live all over it, even on the side a globe shows upside down. What keeps the people there from falling off into space?
choices: A pull toward Earth's centre
The weight of the air above them
The pull of Earth's magnetism
The push of Earth's spin
questions.context: Earth's gravity pulls everything toward the centre of the planet, so down always means toward the centre, wherever a person stands; on the far side of the globe, down is still the ground under their feet. The air, Earth's magnetism and Earth's spin do not hold anyone on.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-PS2-1 asks 5th graders to argue that Earth's gravity pulls objects down, meaning toward the centre of the round Earth.

questions.question: A book has rested on a high shelf, perfectly still, for a whole year. Is Earth's gravity still pulling on it?
questions.answer: Yes, just as hard as if it were falling
choices: Yes, just as hard as if it were falling
No, gravity stops once a thing is still
No, the shelf blocks gravity's pull
Only a little, since it is not moving
questions.context: Gravity pulls on everything all the time, moving or not, so it pulls the resting book down as hard as it would pull a falling one. The book stays put because the shelf holds it up.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders learn that Earth's gravity pulls every object toward Earth (NGSS 5-PS2-1), and the Science Learning Hub names 'gravity only acts on falling objects' as a common belief to correct.

questions.question: A boy leans on a heavy crate of books and pushes with all his strength, but it does not budge. Why does the crate stay still?
questions.answer: The floor pushes back on it just as hard
choices: The floor pushes back on it just as hard
The air around it holds it in place
His push is too weak to be a force
No push can move a crate that heavy
questions.context: A push that moves nothing is still a force. Friction from the floor pushes back against the boy's push, just as hard, so the forces on the crate are balanced and it stays put; a harder push, or a few friends pushing with him, would get it sliding.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.13.4: when a force is applied to an object and it does not move, an opposing force from its surroundings balances it.
